unit.title: Daily Life in the Present Tense

lesson.title: Speed-Talks: 90 Seconds on Your Daily Life
lesson.subject: spanish

contentBlocks.text: This week closes the way real fluency actually gets built: out loud, under a small amount of time pressure, using language you've practiced but didn't memorize word-for-word. Ninety seconds is short enough to demand real command of the present-tense system, and long enough to actually say something true.

The rules are simple: talk about your daily life — entre semana and on weekends — for 90 seconds, using yesterday's paragraph as your foundation, not your script. You may glance at it before you start, but you may not read it aloud line by line; the goal is speaking from what you actually know, the way you'll eventually need to in any real conversation. While you talk, your listener's only job is to notice — and write down — every connector you use (además, en cambio, por eso), plus any soler + infinitive sentence you build in real time.

This is also a moment to notice how far the week actually took you. Monday you had four separate grammar topics; today you're describing your actual cotidiano life using all four at once, without stopping to think about which category a verb belongs to. That's what a system is for: it disappears into fluency once you actually know it.

Whatever your 90 seconds actually covered — a full week or just two contrasting days — the point wasn't a perfect performance, it was proving the system holds together under real, spontaneous use. Next week: describing the world around you — places, cities, neighborhoods — with ser, estar, and haber.

items.prompt: Translate to Spanish: to usually do
Translate to Spanish: to wake up very early
Translate to Spanish: to make the most of

objectives: Deliver a 90-second spoken description of weekday and weekend routines without reading a script line by line
Identify and record the connectors (además, en cambio, por eso) used in a peer's or family member's spoken description
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Complete the vocabulary-recap activity as a warm-up.
2. Explain the ground rules: 90 seconds, glancing at yesterday's paragraph is fine, reading it aloud line by line is not.
3. If working one-on-one, both people deliver a short speed-talk and the listener notes connectors used; in a small group, rotate speakers with a visible timer.
4. Complete the worksheet's before/during/after structure.
5. Preview next week's topic: describing your world with ser, estar, and haber.
differentiationTips: Struggling: allow a written list of 3-4 key phrases (not full sentences) as a memory aid, rather than requiring fully unscripted speech
Ready for more: challenge them to work in one sentence using a category from Monday's map they haven't used yet this week (e.g., an e→i stem-changing verb like pedir or seguir)
If no second person is available, have the student record their own 90 seconds, then replay it and complete the worksheet's listening questions about their own talk
teacherGuide.answerKey: There is no single correct 90-second talk — evaluate for spontaneous (not read-aloud) use of the present-tense system, at least one soler + infinitive sentence, and correct identification of the connectors a partner used.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Closes the week's WA-WL-2015.1.3 (Presentational Speaking) arc with a timed, substantially spontaneous spoken task — per the scope-and-sequence's Day 5 target ('speed-talks — 90 seconds on your daily life; peers note the connectors you used'). Requiring the student to speak from, not read, yesterday's paragraph is what makes this presentational rather than simple recitation.

worksheet.title: Speed-Talks: 90 Seconds on Your Daily Life

generationData.instructions: Use this sheet before, during, and after today's speed-talk.

rows.problem: Before your speed-talk: reread yesterday's paragraph once, then set it aside. Circle any verb form you want to double-check before you speak.
Write one soler + infinitive sentence you plan to say during your 90 seconds that ISN'T already in yesterday's paragraph.
As you listen to someone else's speed-talk, write down every connector (además, en cambio, por eso) you hear them use.
Looking back at this whole week, which category (regular, stem-changing, reflexive, or irregular yo-form) do you still want more practice with, and why?
